summary: The human brain is the substrate for every thought, movement, perception, and emotion we have. The person trusted to operate on it carries that responsibility into every decision — long hours in the OR, precision demanded at every turn. But too much of a clinician's day is still spent on everything around the care. From intraoperative judgment calls to the documentation and coordination that follow, that's the daily calculus for a neurosurgeon — and AI now has an opportunity to help with both. Healthcare is a multi-trillion dollar industry largely built on workflows designed decades ago. Data lives on different systems, on paper, or in a surgeon's head. The technology to capture clinical notes during surgery, interpret medical imaging, and forecast how a mass might evolve — that's not science fiction. It's possible. But possible and deployed are two very different things. In this episode, AWS's Randi Larsen sits down with Dr. Chetan Bettegowda, the Harvey Cushing Professor and Director of Neurosurgery at Johns Hopkins, and Dr. Diego Socolinsky, who leads generative AI for the Americas at AWS and has spent 25 years moving AI from research into production — including deep roots in medical imaging and computer vision. summary: Can you trust what your AI agent does? In this [DATE] episode of GenerAIly Speaking, hosts Jay Busch and Bharathi Srinivasan answer that question twice with live demos, once for an agent in software and once for an agent with arms, a camera and a voice. First, Raviteja Sunkavalli shows how to observe an AI agent from its first prototype through production with Amazon CloudWatch Omni. He traces and evaluates an agent in the IDE while he builds it, sends telemetry with Agent Observability (ADOT SDK), walks the application map, triggers a real failure live, follows it from metrics to traces to logs, and asks Omni to investigate in plain language. He closes the loop by adding the failing case to the evaluation dataset so it is caught before the next release. Next, Jeremy Wallace shows Rad, an agentic AI companion robot he built with Strands Agents, Amazon Bedrock and AWS IoT Greengrass. A Strands agent runs inside ROS 2, reasons and sees with Amazon Bedrock, speaks with Amazon Polly, remembers people, and asks before it moves while a digital twin previews the motion. You also see how AWS IoT Greengrass deploys it to the robot with short-lived credentials, so no AWS keys live on the robot, and how an AI coding agent helped design everything from the code to the 3D-printed body. summary: In this episode of Napkin to MVP, Michael Louis, the founder of Cerebrium, shares how a frustrating reality in 2021, fragile ML tooling with no blueprints for building machine learning products, became the spark for a serverless infrastructure platform that helps companies build and scale AI applications globally. It's the unpolished story of going from an idea on a napkin to a platform powering everything from fine-tuning LLMs to real-time avatars at massive scale. The team went from idea to initial MVP in 6 to 8 weeks, driven by a simple principle: validate or invalidate the idea as quickly as possible, then iterate. Their first major customer, a well-funded company building real-time avatars, pushed the platform to mature fast across reliability, performance, and service quality. That customer is still with them today. AWS was the foundation from day one. The team chose AWS for its reliability and the core primitives they needed, including EC2 and Route 53, calling it ""a safe bet"" that let them focus on building the platform layer on top. This is what building with AI on AWS looks like for startups: turning broken tooling into infrastructure that makes AI accessible to companies of all sizes, so every team can build and scale without stitching together fragile parts. summary: Sovereignty is a priority in boardrooms across Europe, and leaders want it alongside resilience and innovation. At @AWS we’re constantly holding ourselves to deliver all three. That’s why I was so struck by how @Frans Woelders, COO at @Danske Bank, approaches it. He openly says sovereignty is the topic most likely to keep him up at night. Still, he keeps a nuanced view, weighing physical safety, resilience and risk to find the right balance for his organisation. For me, resilience is the word that matters most here. It ran through our conversation, from how Frans protects day to day operations while transforming a bank founded in 1871, to how he’s helping his teams adopt AI at pace. Frans, thank you for such an open and thoughtful conversation.
